headline: Put out every forest fire, get bigger ones
dek: Ferdinand Silcox, US Forest Service, 1935 to 1978.

portrait.alt: Ferdinand Silcox, white-haired, in a dark suit, seated at a desk beside a US flag in a studio surrounded by lights
portrait.credit: Ferdinand A. Silcox, Chief of the Forest Service, Washington, DC, 1933. US Forest Service. Public domain.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Never another 1910
slides.text: In 1910 fires burned more than 3 million acres and killed at least 85 people. **Ferdinand Silcox argued fire could be kept out.**

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Out by 10 a.m.
slides.text: In 1935 Silcox, now chief, ordered every fire controlled by 10 a.m. the next morning. **Yearly acres burned on western national forests fell from 455,340 to 141,975.**

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: The fuel stayed
slides.statLabel: US acres burned a year, 1985 to 1994 vs. 2016 to 2025 (NIFC)
slides.text: Small fires had kept dry pine forests open. Without them, **fuel piled up for bigger, hotter fires.** Climate and building near forests add to it.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Partly
slides.text: In 1943 Harold Weaver warned that keeping all fire out was harming pine forests. **How much fuel would pile up took decades to show.**

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Putting fire back
slides.text: The Forest Service dropped the rule in 1978. **Now it burns and thins forests on purpose.** A 2022 plan targets up to 20 million more acres.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Western national forest acres burned a year: 455,340 (1926 to 1934) to 141,975 (1935 to 1943) (Loveridge, 1944)
No long-running blowup fire on western national forests, 1935 to 1944, the agency reported
Area burned a fraction of its historical extent by the 1950s and 1960s (US Forest Service)
costs: Dry pine stands of 40 to 60 trees an acre grown to hundreds in many places (US Forest Service)
US acres burned a year: 3.0 million (1985 to 1994) to 7.1 million (2016 to 2025), with climate and building also at work (NIFC)
Fire took 52% of the Forest Service budget in 2015, up from 16% in 1995 (USDA)
slides.text: It stopped the fires of its day. **It also stored their fuel for bigger fires later.**

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: The risk piles up
slides.text: Every small fire put out left its fuel standing. So the few that escaped **burned through decades of stored fuel.**

slides.label: Lesson
slides.title: What we take from it
slides.text: Small failures can be doing a job nobody wrote down. **Before you stop them all, ask what they were clearing.**
